summary: Most hypotheses are biologically and clinically plausible and well-specified, with detailed validation plans and careful confounding awareness. However, the IST-3 subset here (n≈200) gives limited power for interaction testing; many subgroups will be small, producing wide CIs and unstable estimates. Priority should be given to hypotheses with strong prior evidence and clear clinical actionability (particularly NIHSS-defined severity bands), while weight- and glucose-based interactions are plausible and actionable but likely underpowered in this dataset and thus should be treated as hypothesis-generating unless supported by pooled/replicated analyses.

scored_hypotheses.title: Moderate benefit of IV alteplase in middle-aged acute ischemic stroke patients (age 50-69)
strengths: Clear, operational subgroup (50–69 years) and a specific, falsifiable claim.
Rationale aligns with known age-related changes in frailty, hemorrhagic risk and recovery potential.
Comprehensive validation plan including continuous-age interactions and sensitivity analyses.
weaknesses: With total N≈200, the 50–69 stratum may be small, limiting power and estimate stability.
Age is a proxy for many correlated factors (frailty, imaging core size) that may not be fully captured in IST-3 covariates.
Not highly novel — reiterates known age trend — so positive finding would need replication before changing practice.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Hypothesis is well-specified and plausible with appropriate planned analyses; but given limited sample size and overlapping known findings about age, this analysis is useful and hypothesis-generating rather than definitive.

scored_hypotheses.title: Older patients (70-79) have reduced but still positive net benefit from IV alteplase at 6 months
strengths: Biologically and clinically plausible with prior trial/registry signals supporting attenuated absolute benefit with age.
Validation plan includes appropriate adjusted/doubly robust estimators and safety checks (sICH, mortality).
Clear subgroup definition and sensitivity analyses proposed (continuous modeling, time windows).
weaknesses: Small subgroup sizes will yield wide CIs and poor power for interaction tests.
Trial selection may preferentially enrol fitter older patients (healthy enrollee bias), limiting generalizability.
Novelty limited; result would primarily contextualize magnitude rather than change understanding.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Clinically relevant and methodologically sound for exploratory analysis; expected to reproduce known trends but will be underpowered for definitive claims in this dataset.

scored_hypotheses.title: Younger-elderly (age 60-69) derive the greatest net benefit-to-risk from IV alteplase in acute ischemic stroke
strengths: Well-argued mechanistic rationale balancing recovery potential and bleeding risk.
Validation plan includes net-benefit calculations and continuous-age modelling to avoid arbitrary cutpoints.
Clear subgroup and covariate set for adjustment.
weaknesses: Overlap with neighboring age-band hypotheses — may produce correlated and redundant findings.
Moderate novelty and likely limited events in 60–69 band with n≈200, reducing precision.
Net-benefit depends on chosen weights for harms which are subjective; sensitivity analyses required.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Plausible and clinically relevant; use IST-3 to generate an estimate and priors for pooling, but interpret results cautiously due to sample size and overlap with other age bands.

scored_hypotheses.title: Moderate NIHSS (5-14) experience greatest absolute benefit from IV alteplase
strengths: Strong biological and empirical support; this severity range is known to maximize absolute benefit in many pooled analyses.
Subgroup rule is clear and operationalizable; planned analyses are rigorous (continuous NIHSS, splines, adjusted/doubly-robust methods).
Direct clinical relevance — could inform practice and patient selection if supported by robust estimates or pooled evidence.
weaknesses: IST-3 subset (n≈200) may limit precision; exact subgroup counts and events may be small.
Potential for misclassification due to NIHSS inter-rater variability; must report event counts and CIs rather than overinterpretation.
Not novel — primary value here is replication/quantification rather than discovery.
scored_hypotheses.justification: This hypothesis is highly testable, clinically actionable, and supported by prior literature; even exploratory IST-3 results will be informative for pooled meta-analysis and should be prioritized.

scored_hypotheses.title: Mild baseline NIHSS (≤4) have limited absolute benefit from IV alteplase
strengths: Clear clinical question with high relevance (debate exists about thrombolysis in minor stroke).
Good validation strategy including harm estimation (sICH) and sensitivity to NIHSS encoding.
Strong conceptual plausibility (ceiling effects, low absolute room for improvement).
weaknesses: May be underpowered in IST-3 subset — minor stroke subgroup often small and events rare.
Heterogeneity within 'mild' strokes (disabling vs non-disabling deficits) necessitates careful sub-stratification which may not be feasible with small N.
Potential for measurement misclassification moving patients across the threshold.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Clinically important and methodologically well-formulated; IST-3 data can meaningfully contribute to evidence synthesis even if underpowered to be definitive.

scored_hypotheses.title: Severe baseline NIHSS (>=15) predicts lower absolute benefit of IV alteplase for 6-month independence
strengths: Strong clinical and mechanistic plausibility (large core, higher sICH risk); widely considered in practice.
Validation plan appropriately includes harm analyses and continuous NIHSS modelling.
Subgroup is clearly defined with standard threshold used in literature.
weaknesses: Small numbers in severe category within a 200-patient sample may produce very imprecise estimates.
Contemporary relevance limited by endovascular therapy availability — generalizability to current practice should be cautious.
Threshold-based dichotomization may hide continuous trends; reliance on dichotomy must be supplemented by continuous analysis.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Clinically salient and well-supported hypothesis; given its direct implications for triage and expected strong prior, should be prioritized for estimation and later pooled analysis.

scored_hypotheses.title: Very high body weight (>=100 kg) reduces benefit of IV alteplase (effect modification by weight)
strengths: Strong pharmacologic plausibility due to dose-capping at an absolute maximum; actionable if true.
Detailed validation plan including mediation by mg/kg dose and continuous-weight splines.
Clear subgroup rule tied to a mechanistic exposure (dose-per-kg) rather than an arbitrary demographic.
weaknesses: Likely very small number of ≥100 kg patients in a 200-person sample; limited power and unstable estimates.
Weight may be estimated in acute settings (measurement error) and documentation of actual dose administered may be incomplete.
Evidence from trials is sparse — positive result would require replication and pharmacokinetic support before practice change.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Plausible, novel and clinically actionable, but IST-3 sample is likely underpowered — treat findings as exploratory and prioritize pooling with other datasets or pharmaco-kinetic analyses.

scored_hypotheses.title: Low body weight (<60 kg) modifies net benefit of IV alteplase—higher harm / lower probability of OHS 0-2 at 6 months
strengths: Biologically plausible links to frailty and physiologic reserve; dosing and outcome mechanisms are described.
Comprehensive validation plan including mediation for sICH and continuous-weight analyses.
Operational subgroup is straightforward if weight is reliably recorded.
weaknesses: Absolute low-weight counts may be small; sex confounding (threshold captures more women) must be addressed robustly.
Low-weight is a marker for frailty/chronic illness — residual confounding likely even after adjustment.
Limited direct evidence base; findings should be validated externally.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Worth evaluating as hypothesis-generating given clinical plausibility, but conclusions from IST-3 alone will be limited; consider pooling with other datasets.

scored_hypotheses.title: Moderate body weight (60-99 kg) modifies benefit from IV alteplase for acute ischemic stroke
strengths: Reasonable synthesis of pharmacologic dosing rationale (mid-range weight avoids capping) and clinical recovery potential.
Validation includes dose-per-kg mediation checks and continuous-weight modelling.
Clear three-category weight bins that map to dosing rules.
weaknesses: Hypothesis is derivative of extremes (<60 and >=100 kg) and offers limited incremental insight if extremes are already tested.
Mid-weight band likely contains the majority of patients; any observed benefit may reflect baseline prognostic differences rather than pharmacology.
Evidence is indirect; measurement error in weight and confounding by BMI/composition not fully captured.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Operational and testable, but less novel; useful as part of a broader weight-effect exploration, interpreted cautiously given sample size and correlated hypotheses.

scored_hypotheses.title: Marked admission hyperglycaemia (glucose >= 10 mmol/L) attenuates benefit of IV alteplase
strengths: Strong pathophysiologic rationale and consistent observational evidence linking high glucose to worse outcomes and increased sICH after reperfusion.
Validation plan is thorough (continuous glucose modelling, adjustment for diabetes/HbA1c if available, harm mediation).
Clear operational cutpoint and sensitivity analyses recommended.
weaknesses: Distinguishing stress hyperglycaemia from chronic hyperglycaemia (no HbA1c) may be difficult; residual confounding by severity is possible.
High-glucose subgroup may be small, limiting precision of interaction tests.
Heterogeneity of glucose measurement timing and method (capillary vs lab) can introduce misclassification.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Biologically plausible and clinically relevant; IST-3 can contribute to pooled evidence though alone it may be underpowered to settle interaction conclusively.

scored_hypotheses.title: Admission hypoglycaemia (glucose < 4 mmol/L) predicts worse 6‑month functional outcome and may modify alteplase effect if given before correction
strengths: Clear clinical safety rationale — current practice recommends correction prior to thrombolysis.
Validation plan sensibly distinguishes randomized interaction from the observational question of correction timing.
Potentially high clinical relevance if hypoglycaemia is not routinely corrected before alteplase in some settings.
weaknesses: Very low prevalence of admission hypoglycaemia in stroke trials — extremely limited power in IST-3 subset (n≈200).
Much of the causal question (effect of giving alteplase before vs after correction) is observational and confounded.
Evidence base is sparse; findings would be hypothesis-generating and require careful interpretation.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Although clinically sensible and biologically plausible, rarity of exposure and observational nature of correction-timing analyses make this low priority for definitive testing in this dataset.

scored_hypotheses.title: Moderate admission hyperglycaemia (6–9 mmol/L) preserves or does not reduce benefit from IV alteplase
strengths: Addresses a clinically relevant nuance — most patients with mild-to-moderate hyperglycaemia may still benefit from thrombolysis.
Validation plan is comprehensive (continuous glucose modelling, stratification by diabetes, time-to-treatment).
Operational subgroup is easy to implement if glucose data are reliable.
weaknesses: Potential confounding by severity and diabetes status; evidence is mixed across studies.
Moderate glucose band may include heterogeneous patients (chronic vs stress hyperglycaemia).
IST-3 sample size may be insufficient for precise interaction estimation.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Worth exploring as it has direct clinical implications (avoiding unnecessary withholding of alteplase), though findings should be treated as exploratory and combined with other cohorts for inference.

scored_hypotheses.title: Higher baseline GCS (>=13) predicts greater benefit from IV alteplase
strengths: GCS is a simple bedside measure that correlates with global stroke severity and is readily available.
Analytic plan includes adjustment for NIHSS and sensitivity checks; plausible biologic rationale.
Operational definition is clear and analyses are feasible.
weaknesses: GCS correlates strongly with NIHSS and other severity markers — disentangling independent modification by GCS is challenging.
GCS can be affected by sedation/intubation and measurement variability, introducing misclassification.
Evidence-specific novelty is modest; main value is replication/quantification.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Reasonable and testable; results may help triage decisions but must be interpreted alongside NIHSS and imaging data.

scored_hypotheses.title: Low baseline GCS (<=8) predicts limited benefit or net harm from IV alteplase in acute ischemic stroke
strengths: Clinically important subgroup (coma/severe depressed consciousness) with clear rationale for reduced salvageability and higher hemorrhagic risk.
Validation plan addresses harms, competing risks and withdrawal-of-care confounding.
Clear operational definition and sensible sensitivity analyses (exclude sedated/intubated).
weaknesses: Small expected counts in this stratum in a 200-patient sample limit inference and create unstable estimates.
Low GCS is heterogeneous (intoxication, metabolic causes) requiring careful case selection.
Findings may reflect withdrawal-of-care patterns rather than causal effect modification.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Important safety-relevant hypothesis; IST-3 can provide exploratory estimates but larger pooled analyses needed for reliable inference.

scored_hypotheses.title: Fully alert patients (GCS == 15) have limited absolute benefit from alteplase due to ceiling effects
strengths: Clear, operational subgroup and a well-understood mechanism (ceiling effect) for smaller ARD.
Validation plan includes absolute- and relative-scale analyses, prognostic calibration and HTE methods.
Direct clinical relevance for decision-making in minor stroke.
weaknesses: GCS==15 does not guarantee non-disabling deficits — reliance on GCS alone can be misleading without NIHSS/focal deficit details.
Potentially limited power and multiple-testing risk across related severity hypotheses.
Threshold is somewhat arbitrary; results must be complemented with continuous/severity-specific analysis.
scored_hypotheses.justification: Practical and testable hypothesis that complements NIHSS-based analyses; exploratory IST-3 results can guide meta-analytic synthesis and clinical framing of minor-stroke decisions.

top_hypotheses: Moderate NIHSS (5-14) experience greatest absolute benefit from IV alteplase
Mild baseline NIHSS (≤4) have limited absolute benefit from IV alteplase
Severe baseline NIHSS (>=15) predicts lower absolute benefit of IV alteplase for 6-month independence
methodological_concerns: Limited total sample size (n≈200) — many subgroups will have small N and very wide confidence intervals; prioritize estimation and CIs over dichotomous significance testing.

Multiple correlated subgroup tests (age bands, NIHSS bins, weight bins, glucose bands, GCS splits) increase false-positive risk; control for multiplicity or treat results as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

Measurement error in key covariates (weight estimates, point-of-care glucose vs lab, NIHSS inter-rater variability, GCS affected by sedation) can bias subgroup classification and attenuate or distort interaction tests.

Changes in standard care since IST-3 (widespread endovascular therapy, selection imaging) limit direct applicability of some subgroup findings (notably high NIHSS / LVO-related hypotheses) to contemporary practice.

Subgroup analyses in randomized trials are observational contrasts; within-stratum imbalance, selection bias (per-protocol analyses), and collider bias (conditioning on post-randomization variables) must be explicitly guarded against with ITT-based and doubly-robust methods.

Recommendation: where possible, combine IST-3 estimates with other trials/registries via individual-patient-data meta-analysis or hierarchical Bayesian pooling to obtain stable, generalizable subgroup effect estimates.
